body.text: In October, well-known Taiwanese television host Kevin Tsai, popular on both sides of the Taiwan Strait, was spotted by the media attending a campaign event for Puma Shen, a legislator running for mayor of Taipei. Given Tsai’s popularity in China, his appearance quickly sparked criticism. The incumbent Taipei mayor, Chiang Wan-an, helped defuse the controversy by inviting Tsai to the opening of his own campaign headquarters. Three weeks after attending Shen’s campaign event, Tsai publicly stated that he had never supported Taiwanese independence and that his work required him to interact with people holding a range of political views. The following day, he attended Chiang’s campaign event.
If attending a rally is tantamount to declaring one’s support for Taiwan’s future, imagine what will be made of the November 28 vote.

Shen, the candidate of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), has spent years studying Chinese influence operations and promoting civilian preparedness in Taiwan. Chinese authorities have opened an investigation into him on allegations of secession. Chiang, the Kuomintang (KMT) incumbent, has maintained an open channel of communication between officials in Taipei and Shanghai. Beijing and Washington may be tempted to interpret a Shen victory as a vote for independence or a Chiang victory as a turn toward China. Either interpretation, however, would link a municipal election to an issue that Taipei’s voters have not been asked to vote on.

Consider an exchange during the October 31 debate between Shen and Chiang. Chiang challenged Shen to explain why two redevelopment projects, one in Datong and the other in Neihu, had stalled. Chiang attributed the delays to restrictions on building heights near Taipei’s Songshan Airport. Shen fired back with a question of his own: If city officials knew about these restrictions, why hadn’t they explained them to residents from the outset? Chiang used the exchange to question his challenger’s command of city affairs. Shen, in turn, used it to ask what good that expertise did residents if they learned about an obstacle too late to do anything about it.

The most important takeaway from their heated exchanges, however, is not what the candidates said, but what they left unsaid. China, the elephant in the room when it comes to cross-strait relations, was not raised even once as a key issue during the two-hour debate.

That encapsulates the kind of local issues Taipei voters will actually base their decision on. Some might vote for Chiang, crediting him with moving other difficult projects forward, including one at Nanjichang Night Market. Others might favor Shen’s proposal to screen older buildings for earthquake risks and to help residents arrange repairs. Two homeowners could vote for different candidates – while holding precisely the same views about China. The election night count offers no way to tell.

Taipei’s recent electoral history illustrates the limits of interpreting local elections through the lens of national politics – and vice versa. In 2022, the city elected Chiang as mayor. Just over a year later, in the presidential election, the DPP’s Lai Ching-te carried Taipei, edging out the KMT’s Hou Yu-ih by just 641 votes. Chiang’s mayoral victory would therefore have been a poor guide to the city’s presidential preferences. There is even less reason to interpret a vote in the capital as evidence of a broader change of heart across Taiwan for or against a political party – or that party’s approach to China.

True, the result will shape national politics. Winning Taipei would give Shen a larger audience for his work on civilian defense. A second term would give Chiang greater standing within the KMT to make the case for engagement with Shanghai, and possibly Beijing. Plus, the Taipei mayorship has in the past served as a launching pad for presidential ambitions. Winning office gives a politician the chance to advance causes that may have had little to do with why voters chose him.

The election’s outcome could certainly also influence cross-strait relations. During Chiang’s tenure, the Taipei–Shanghai Twin-City Forum has kept officials from the two cities in contact. A Chiang victory would give him another term to pursue those exchanges. A Shen victory would test the conditions under which they can continue. Although Shen has criticized the forum’s value, he has said he would attend if it offered practical benefits and came without political preconditions. On October 14, Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office dismissed his offer, citing his alleged support for independence.

Suppose Shen wins, repeats his offer, and finds Shanghai unwilling to meet with him. Concluding that Taipei voters chose to sever contact would erase Beijing’s role in the decision. The reverse inference – that vote for Chiang implies approval of his engagement with Chinese officials – would be equally questionable. A Taipei resident might value Chiang’s ability to keep municipal officials talking while still opposing closer political ties. Wanting the conversation with Shanghai to continue is entirely compatible with wanting Beijing to have less say in Taiwan’s affairs.

Local governance is undoubtedly important for the stability of the Taiwan Strait. Taipei’s city government, for example, helps residents prepare for an air raid, down to practicing how to reach shelter when the sirens sound. How well the city carries out that work matters regardless of which party holds power. Still, it’s not going to be an issue that is top of mind when Taipei residents fill out their ballots.

On November 28, Taipei’s voters will choose who takes responsibility for the safety of their homes, the city’s readiness for an emergency, and its dealings with Shanghai. Beijing and Washington have good reason to pay close attention to what the next mayor does with that authority. But anyone claiming a mandate for independence or unification is looking for evidence the mayoral count cannot provide.
